title: Mirabel and the Portrait
premise: Emrys Winterbourne has spent two decades as a hospice nurse in the village of Hollowmere, rationalizing the counting voices they hear from the dying and the wet, dragging sounds beneath the old Ashcombe estate. When an excavation crew unseals a door bricked shut from the inside in 1974, the estate's buried history—nine villagers lured down the well by the portrait of a long-dead matriarch, and Emrys's own grandmother's role in sealing them—comes flooding back. The portrait, recovered and hung in the hospice, begins choosing new sitters, and Emrys realizes the well refills each generation unless what was taken—a child's name, written and stolen—is returned. In the climax, Emrys descends through the door, confronts the portrait's hunger, and gives back the name at the cost of their own reflection, breaking the cycle but leaving them faceless in every mirror, finally seen by everyone and no one.
about_author: Silas Thornbury is the pen name of a former mortuary attendant who spent eleven years in rural care facilities across the Welsh borders before turning to writing. Their fiction draws on overheard deathbed confessions and the folklore of sealed wells, and they insist they have never looked at a family portrait the same way since.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Emrys, a hospice nurse, tends to dying Mrs. Prewitt, who counts backwards in her sleep and whispers about 'the lady in the frame.' Emrys hears the counting harmonize with a second voice beneath the floorboards. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as professional routine; the reader learns Emrys has explained away these sounds for twenty years.

chapters.title: What the Excavator Found
chapters.summary: A crew digging foundations for a hospice extension unearths an iron door, sealed from the inside with mortar and, oddly, a child's handprint pressed into the wet cement. That night Emrys hears the counting stop mid-number for the first time. POV: Emrys, with a brief interlude from foreman Denny Cole. Emotional beat: the rational explanations begin to fail.

chapters.title: The Ashcombe Portrait
chapters.summary: Among the estate's salvaged effects is a portrait of Cordelia Ashcombe, whose eyes seem to follow the ward. Patients begin requesting it be moved out of the common room; then begin requesting to sit before it. Emrys finds their grandmother's name in the estate's 1974 visitor ledger. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: personal history intrudes; the horror becomes inheritance.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Hands
chapters.summary: Emrys searches their late grandmother's belongings and finds a journal describing the 1974 sealing: nine villagers taken by 'the lady below,' a stolen christening record, and a bargain made to keep the well quiet for one generation. The journal ends mid-sentence. POV: Emrys, interleaved with the grandmother's journal entries. Emotional beat: guilt across generations; love and duty pulling apart.

chapters.title: Sitters
chapters.summary: The portrait claims its first new sitter: Denny Cole, found at the bricked door, having dug at it bare-handed until his nails split, counting backwards. The hospice administrator wants the painting burned; Emrys, touching the frame, hears nine voices instead of two. POV: Emrys and Denny in alternating sections. Emotional beat: escalation—the portrait is not passive.

chapters.title: The Name That Was Taken
chapters.summary: Emrys decodes the journal: the stolen thing is a name—Cordelia's daughter's, erased from every record so the portrait could wear it. The well refills each time the name is spoken by someone who doesn't know it's borrowed. Emrys realizes their own middle name is the erased one. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: identity crisis; Emrys has been the inheritance all along.

chapters.title: Refilling
chapters.summary: The well beneath the hospice begins to rise—water in the basement, wet footprints on the stairs, patients waking to count aloud in unison. The portrait's Cordelia now has Emrys's face. The village's oldest resident confirms the 1974 bargain expires at the solstice, three days away. POV: Emrys, with village chorus sections. Emotional beat: the town's complicity surfaces; isolation becomes solidarity.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Emrys's partner, Ruth, begs them to run; the journal's final page reveals the sealing required a Winterbourne to stay behind. Emrys, who has spent twenty years being invisible—unnoticed, unremarkable—understands the portrait chose them because no one would miss a sitter. They choose to go anyway, for the nine below and for Ruth. POV: Emrys and Ruth. Emotional beat: the cost made intimate; love as the reason, not the obstacle.

chapters.title: Through the Door
chapters.summary: At solstice midnight, Emrys unseals the door from the outside and descends the well stair into a flooded hall where the nine wait, mid-count, and Cordelia's portrait hangs at the bottom, larger than any frame could hold. Emrys speaks the daughter's true name aloud, and the portrait begins to drink their reflection to replace it. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: climax—sacrifice, terror, and a terrible tenderness toward the hungry dead.

chapters.title: The Empty Frame
chapters.summary: Emrys wakes on the well stair; below, the hall is dry and the nine are gone, the frame empty except for a handprint matching the one in the 1974 mortar. Emrys returns to the hospice, where mirrors show them blurred and patients' counting has stopped. Ruth sees them anyway. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: resolution—power renounced, inheritance ended, and a quiet, faceless peace.
